```{python}
for t in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):                   # same moment, two men: how far apart the chaser still is
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P(R0 + vR * t), P(chase[int(round(t / dt))])
    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (1, 1.2)), zorder=5.5)
    xr, yr = P(R0 + vR * t + np.array([0.0, 0.9]))
    ax.text(xr, yr, f"{t:.1f} s: {GAP[t]:.1f} yd", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center",
            zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
spot(f, p, MEET[0], MEET[1], ms=9)
solid(f, p, [(8.0, 14.6), (MEET[0] + 1.6, MEET[1] + 2.2)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4)
point_to(f, p, (2.0, 11.4), tuple(chase[45]), "chase (grey):\naimed at the man", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, MEET[0] - 0.4, MEET[1] - 4.6, "angle: aimed where\nhe will be, a step inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, over_end[0] - 1.9, over_end[1] + 1.2, "overrun", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, cut0[0] + 4.4, cut0[1] - 2.8, "cutback", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.7, 15.6, "leverage player:\nstays outside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, -0.9, 9.4, "the back bounces\noutside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

@fig-pursuit makes the point with real geometry. A linebacker who runs *at* the back (the grey path) is
always aiming at a spot the back has already left. In this example the linebacker is the faster man, and he
is still two yards behind after a second and a half; he gets within arm's reach only after
`{python} f"{CATCH_T:.1f}"` seconds, `{python} f"{CATCH_D:.0f}"` yards downfield. Against a back who is as fast as he
is, or faster, which in the open field is most backs, he never catches him at all. A linebacker who aims at *where the
back will be* (orange) cuts the distance he has to run and meets the back in about a second and a quarter.
That is a pursuit angle. The catch is the dashed path: aim too far ahead, and the linebacker gets outside the
back, who simply plants his foot and cuts back behind him. Every defender who has been run past has done one
of those two things: chased, or overrun.

The rule coaches give for it is *inside-out* again: take the angle that keeps the ball carrier a step *outside*
you, never inside. If you are inside him, he can only go one way, outside, and outside is where the next
defender is.

That next defender is the *leverage player*: the man on the outside whose job is to keep the ball inside,
turning the runner back toward the pursuit. In @fig-pursuit it is the cornerback; on other plays it is the
end who set the edge, an outside linebacker, a safety who came down. (The defense names him in advance, as its
*force* player, in [Run Fits and Box Math](05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).) Put the two together and you
have the shape of good team pursuit: one defender outside the ball, squeezing it in, and everyone else
inside-out on it, each a little deeper and farther inside than the man in front, so that whichever way the
runner cuts, someone is already there. Coaches drill it constantly, and it is one of the clearest things you
can see on the end-zone replay: on a good defense, the arrows all converge.

## Tackling, and why tackles get missed at the second level

Then the linebacker has to bring the man down. Tackling has changed more in the last decade than in the
fifty years before it, for two reasons: safety, and the realization that the old way missed too many
tackles.

The old way, the one a lot of fans still picture, was a head-on collision: eyes up, head across the runner's
body ("head across the bow"), drive through him. It produces highlight hits. It also uses the head as the
first point of contact, and it fails whenever the runner moves at the last moment, because a tackler who
commits his whole body to one spot can't adjust.

The modern approach is [**leverage tackling**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-tackling), and its
most influential teachers were Pete Carroll's Seattle Seahawks. In 2014 they made a 20-minute instructional
video of their shoulder tackling, borrowed from rugby, and that August the league sent it, with a letter from
Carroll, to coaches and parents at every level of the game; a second video in 2015 named its basic tackle the
*hawk tackle*.[^hawk] The ideas fit together:

- **Leverage first.** The tackler approaches with the runner on one side of him, usually inside-out, so the
  runner's only escape is toward the sideline and the next defender. The pursuit angle in @fig-pursuit is the
  start of the tackle, not something separate from it.
- **The near shoulder to the near thigh.** The target is the runner's thighs ("eyes through the thighs," in
  Seattle's coaching points), not his chest; the shoulder makes contact and the head goes to the side, behind
  the runner on a tackle from an angle, out of the line of contact. The legs are what carry the ball,
  and they can't dodge as easily as a torso can.
- **Wrap and roll.** Arms around the thighs, keep the feet moving, and roll the runner to the ground, taking
  him toward the help rather than trying to drive him backward.
- **Breakdown in space.** Within a couple of yards of the runner, the tackler shortens his steps and lowers
  his hips, so he can move either way with the runner's last cut.

The rules have pushed in the same direction. In March 2024 the league banned the
[hip-drop tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hip-drop-tackle), in which
a tackler grabs a runner from behind and swings his hips and weight down onto the runner's legs, with a
15-yard penalty; the details are in [Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).[^hipdrop]
For the 2026 season the league and the players' union added a three-strike system: a player called for three of
five fouls (hip-drop, horse-collar, launching, hits on a defenseless player and blindside blocks) in a season
is suspended for a game.[^threestrike] Most of those fouls are committed by defenders tackling in pursuit,
which is the linebacker's daily life.

### Why the second level is where tackles are made, and missed

Where on the field do linebackers actually tackle people? nflverse's play-by-play records who made the
tackle on every play, so we can ask the data. @fig-tackle-depth sorts every designed run from 2021 to 2025 by how
far the runner got before he was brought down, and shows who made the tackle.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tackle-depth
#| fig-cap: "Who makes the tackle, by how far the run got. Every regular-season designed run from 2021 to 2025 that ended in a tackle (no scrambles, touchdowns or penalties), grouped by the yards gained, with the share of tackles made by each position group (the first tackler listed in nflverse play-by-play, matched to the team's roster position that season). Inside linebackers are those listed ILB, MLB or LB; outside linebackers are those listed OLB, mostly 3-4 edge rushers but also some off-ball 4-3 outside linebackers, so the inside-linebacker line is a floor for off-ball linebackers. The defensive line makes most of the tackles at or near the line. The inside linebackers' share holds at a fifth to a quarter out to 9 yards and peaks on runs of 5 to 9, as the line's share collapses. Past 10 yards it is the defensive backs' tackle."
style.apply()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
ax.axvspan(1.5, 4.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.55, lw=0, zorder=0)
order = ["Defensive line", "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)", "Inside linebacker", "Defensive back"]
cols = {"Defensive line": style.SERIES[3], "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)": style.SERIES[4],
        "Inside linebacker": style.SERIES[1], "Defensive back": style.SERIES[0]}
xs = np.arange(len(BIN_LABELS))
LABEL_Y = {"Defensive line": SHARE["Defensive line"].values[-1] - 2.5,
           "Outside linebacker (mostly edge)": SHARE["Outside linebacker (mostly edge)"].values[-1] + 1.0,
           "Inside linebacker": SHARE["Inside linebacker"].values[-1] + 2.5}
for g in order:
    lw = 2.6 if g == "Inside linebacker" else 1.6
    ax.plot(xs, SHARE[g].values, marker="o", ms=3.5, lw=lw, color=cols[g], zorder=3)
    ax.text(xs[-1] + 0.15, LABEL_Y.get(g, SHARE[g].values[-1]), g, va="center", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks(xs, BIN_LABELS)
ax.set_xlabel("Yards gained on the run")
ax.set_ylabel("Share of tackles (%)")
ax.set_xlim(-0.3, len(BIN_LABELS) + 1.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 85)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.text(3.0, 80, "the second level (3-9 yards)", ha="center", fontsize=7.6, color=style.INK_2)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read the chart from left to right and you can watch the three levels hand the runner along. Runs stopped at
or near the line are the defensive line's: about two in five of those tackles. The inside linebackers' share
barely moves, a fifth to a quarter of the tackles on every run up to 9 yards, and it peaks, at about a
quarter, on runs of 5 to 9 yards, just where the line's share collapses. They never top the chart, because
they share the second level with everyone else who flows to the ball, and because the roster labels
undercount them. Past 10 yards the run has beaten them, and it is a defensive back's tackle. Across all runs,
inside linebackers made `{python} f"{LB_SHARE_ALL:.0f}"`% of the tackles; their median tackle came on a run of
`{python} f"{MED['Inside linebacker']:.0f}"` yards, against `{python} f"{MED['Defensive line']:.0f}"` for
linemen and `{python} f"{MED['Defensive back']:.0f}"` for defensive backs.[^tackledata]

One thing in the chart deserves a second look: defensive backs already make
`{python} f"{SHARE.loc['5-6', 'Defensive back']:.0f}"`% of the tackles on runs of only 5 or 6 yards. Those
tackles split almost evenly among cornerbacks (`{python} f"{DB_56['CB']:.0f}"`%), free safeties
(`{python} f"{DB_56['FS']:.0f}"`%) and strong safeties (`{python} f"{DB_56['SS']:.0f}"`%). The corners are the
leverage players on outside runs, turning the ball back in, as in @fig-pursuit; the safeties are the eighth
man in the box when a single-high defense rotates one down, or the "big nickel" safety playing linebacker. The
second level isn't only linebackers any more, which is where the end of this chapter is heading.

The chart is also a warning about the statistic fans quote most. A linebacker's tackle total counts every
tackle the same, but a tackle five yards downfield is a run that beat the defense first, and the best fill of
the game, the one that meets the fullback at the line and makes the back bounce into a teammate, often goes in
the box score under someone else's name. Coaches grade linebackers on whether they were in their gap on time;
the tackle is a by-product.

Missed tackles are not in the play-by-play, but Pro Football Reference charts them for every defender, and
nflverse carries the numbers. Per hundred tackle attempts from 2021 to 2025 (runs and passes together),
defensive linemen missed `{python} f"{MISS['DL']:.1f}"`, inside linebackers `{python} f"{MISS['ILB']:.1f}"`,
outside linebackers `{python} f"{MISS['OLB']:.1f}"`, safeties `{python} f"{MISS['S']:.1f}"` and cornerbacks
`{python} f"{MISS['CB']:.1f}"`.[^misses] The farther from the line a defender usually tackles, the more often
he misses. A lineman tackles a back who is still in a crowd, barely moving, with nowhere to go. Past the line
the runner is moving at full speed, with room to cut both ways, and the tackler is often coming off a block,
from an angle, alone. The runner chooses his cut after seeing the tackler commit; the tackler has to commit
first.

Two things stand out. Inside linebackers make their tackles in far more space than linemen do and miss barely
more often: that is what leverage tackling, and all the drilling behind it, buys. (Take away one direction
with your angle, and you only have to win the other.) And the misses that hurt are the ones past the line,
because the cost of a miss grows with the space behind it: a lineman who misses leaves the back a crowd, a
linebacker who misses leaves him a safety ten yards away.

For a play-by-play look, the 2024 Big Data Bowl was about tackling, and its data marks every missed tackle on
nine weeks of 2022 plays. This chapter's source includes code (not run here, because the data isn't
downloaded) that counts missed-tackle rates by position from it.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (missed tackles by position, Big Data Bowl 2024 data; not run here)"
# Data: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nfl-big-data-bowl-2024/data (tackles.csv, players.csv).
# Check the year's data dictionary; column names below are from the 2024 release.
import pandas as pd
tackles = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2024/tackles.csv")      # gameId, playId, nflId, tackle, assist, forcedFumble, pff_missedTackle
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb2024/players.csv")      # nflId, position, ...
t = tackles.merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId")
by_pos = t.groupby("position").agg(made=("tackle", "sum"), assists=("assist", "sum"),
                                   missed=("pff_missedTackle", "sum"))
by_pos["miss_rate"] = by_pos.missed / (by_pos.made + by_pos.assists + by_pos.missed)
print(by_pos.sort_values("miss_rate", ascending=False))

# To watch one of them: gridiron.bdb.prepare(tracking, plays, game_id, play_id) and show_animation().
```

## Linebackers in coverage

Half the snaps in a game are passes, and on most of them the linebackers are in coverage. Their jobs fall
into three families.

### Zone: the hook/curl defender

In zone coverage, the linebacker drops to an area. The most common linebacker zone is the one between the
offensive tackle and the numbers, about 8 to 12 yards deep, which combines the
[hook zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-zone) over the tackles and the
[curl zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-zone) outside it (both defined in
[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)). A linebacker who drops there is
a [**hook / curl defender**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-curl-defender).

```{python}
#| label: fig-hook-curl
#| fig-cap: "Two linebackers as hook/curl defenders in Cover 3 against a 2x2 formation. Cover 3 has three deep defenders, each taking a third of the field (here the two cornerbacks and the free safety, drawn without zones), and four underneath. On the pass read the Mike and the Will drop to their zones (shaded), about 8 to 10 yards deep, from just outside the offensive tackles toward the slot receivers, opening their hips toward the slot on their side and reading the quarterback. The Mike walls Y's slant: he gets into its path, so the throw has to go around him. The Will's slot receiver, H, runs straight up the seam, so the Will carries him (dashed) to about 12 yards, until the free safety can take over. Then both sink under the curls, eyes on the quarterback."
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 16.0, "Z")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.6, 1.4), will=(4.6, -1.8)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -7.6, "$"), D("SS", "S", 6.5, 10.6, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 14.0, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 16.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.dropback(2.0)
p.route("X", r.go(16)); p.route("Z", r.go(16))
go_to(p, "H", (17.0, -8.2), "route", via=[(4.0, -8.9)])        # the seam
go_to(p, "Y", (6.4, 4.4), "route", via=[(2.4, 9.0)])           # the slant
p.drop("WILL", (8.2, -5.8), zone=(6.0, 7.0), label="hook/curl")
p.drop("MIKE", (7.6, 5.0), zone=(6.0, 7.0), label="hook/curl")
p.drop("FS", (17.5, 0.0)); p.drop("LCB", (16.0, -15.0)); p.drop("RCB", (16.0, 15.0))
p.drop("NB", (6.0, -12.0)); p.drop("SS", (6.0, 13.0))
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.3, lateral=(-19.4, 19.4), window=(-7.4, 20.2), title=False)
dashed(f, p, [(8.4, -6.1), (11.0, -7.0), (13.4, -7.3)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4)
say(f, p, 14.4, -4.4, "Will: carry the\nseam to ~12 yd", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.4, 8.4, "Mike: wall the slant,\nthen sink, eyes on the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

The hook/curl defender's job is a sequence. **First, wall**: get in the path of the slot receiver's inside
route, so the slant or the dig has to go around him. **If the slot runs straight up the seam instead, carry
him**: run with him, inside and underneath, until a deep defender can take over, about 10 to 12 yards
downfield. Four receivers running deep against Cover 3's three [deep thirds](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-third)
is the classic way to beat it, and the hook/curl linebacker's seam carry is what stops it. **Then, sink**: as
the outside receivers push deep, back up under the curls and comebacks. **All the while, eyes on the quarterback**, because a zone defender breaks
on the throw, not on the receiver. Linebackers in modern NFL defenses rarely drop to a fixed spot and wait;
most play some version of [pattern matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching), zone that
turns into man coverage on whichever receiver enters his area. The
[Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) and [Tampa 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)
chapters show the most demanding linebacker drops: in Tampa 2, the Mike runs straight down the middle of the
field to take away the seam, 15 or 20 yards deep.

The model hook defender of the last decade was Seattle's Bobby Wagner, the Mike in the 2013 Seahawks' Cover 3,
behind the Under front of [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd) and in front of a secondary nicknamed the
"Legion of Boom." Watch his early-down drops in Super Bowl XLVIII, a 43–8 win over Denver in which he made ten
tackles: how fast he gets depth, how he walls the crossing routes, and then how his run fills come square and
downhill. He went on to six first-team All-Pro selections, more than two thousand career tackles, and the 2025
Walter Payton Man of the Year award, playing for Washington.[^wagner]

### Man: the back and the tight end, and the hole

In man coverage the linebacker is usually assigned the running back or a tight end. This is where a
linebacker is most exposed. Running backs are quicker than he is and have the whole width of the field; tight
ends are often as fast as he is and bigger. Offenses build plays specifically to get the back in a route
against a linebacker in space, like the *angle* route (a fake to the outside and a break back inside), and to
put a fast tight end on a slow linebacker.

```{python}
#| label: fig-man-hole
#| fig-cap: "Two linebacker jobs in man coverage (Cover 1: one deep safety, everyone else in man). The Will has the running back (dotted line): if the back runs a route, the Will covers him; if the back stays in to block, many defenses let the Will add himself to the rush (a 'green dog' or 'hug'). The Mike has no receiver. He drops to the hole, the middle of the field about 8 to 15 yards deep, reads the quarterback and drives on anything thrown in front of him: the crossing route or the dig that beats man coverage underneath."
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -16.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                       te(+1), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.6, 1.2), will=(4.6, -2.0)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -9.0, "$"), D("SS", "S", 6.0, 6.2, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 14.0, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 2.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 2.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for d_, rec in (("LCB", "X"), ("NB", "H"), ("SS", "Y"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, rec)
p.drop("MIKE", (10.0, 0.0), zone=(6.0, 9.0), label="hole")
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.3, lateral=(-19.4, 19.4), window=(-7.4, 17.6), title=False)
say(f, p, 7.4, -7.0, "Will: man\non the back", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 12.4, 8.8, "Mike: rob the\nmiddle, read the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

The third family is the job in @fig-man-hole: the linebacker with nobody to cover. In man coverage with one
deep safety, the defense often has a spare man, and it can put him in the
[hole zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hole-zone), the middle of the field 8 to 15 yards deep, as a
[robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber) (also called the [rat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rat)).
Staffs use the two words loosely, but many say *rat* for a low hole player, about 5 to 8 yards deep, sitting
on crossers, usually a linebacker, and *robber* for a deeper one, 10 to 12 yards deep, jumping digs and
in-cuts, usually a safety. Crossing routes and digs are how offenses beat man coverage, and they arrive right
there. A linebacker who
reads the quarterback well can make a career out of that spot; Luke Kuechly made a good part of his there.

### Play-action, revisited

[Play-Action, Boots, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) showed play-action
from the offense's side: a fake run that pulls the linebackers forward, and a throw into the space behind them.
Now that you know what a linebacker looks at, you can see why it works, and what the good ones do about it.

The fake is aimed at his keys, his *run-fit triggers*. The linemen fire out low, like a run. The back runs his run path. The quarterback
reaches the ball toward him. Every key says run. But one key can't say it completely, because of a rule: on a
pass, an offensive lineman may not be more than a yard downfield when the ball is thrown. So on play-action,
the linemen who would climb to the linebackers on the real run *can't*. They block at the line and stay there.
A linebacker who keys the back sees a run. A linebacker who keys the uncovered guard, the man who should be
coming for *him* on a run, sees a guard who fires out and then doesn't come. That is the tell.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pa-keys
#| fig-cap: "Play-action from the linebacker's side (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The same play twice: an inside-zone fake to the right and a tight end (Y) running a deep crossing route behind the linebackers, against a 4-2-5 whose Mike (ringed) is over the uncovered right guard. Top row: this Mike keys the back. 1: eyes on the back. 2: the back takes the fake, so the Mike steps up to fill. 3: when the ball is thrown he is five or six yards deep, and Y is behind him. Bottom row: this Mike keys the right guard (green ring). 1: eyes on the guard. 2: the guard fires out but stays at the line instead of climbing to him (a lineman may not go downfield on a pass): no climb, so not a run, and the Mike gets depth. 3: he is about ten yards deep, in the crossing route's path, as the ball is thrown (dashed brown: the throw). The Will drops the same way in both rows; the text says why."
def pa_play(keys_guard):
    off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R")]
    dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.5, 1.8), will=(4.5, -1.0), wide_ends=False)
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in OL_KEYS:                                         # run-action: low first step, then hold
        q = p.players[k]
        go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.4, q.w + 0.35), "block", speed=1.8)
    for k, end in (("WE", (1.1, -4.0)), ("DT", (1.1, -2.1)), ("NT", (1.1, 1.0)), ("SE", (1.1, 4.1))):
        go_to(p, k, end, speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.7, 1.0), speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-7.0, 0.3), speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.2, 3.4), "run", speed=5.5, via=[(-4.2, 2.2)])
    go_to(p, "Y", (12.2, -7.5), "route", speed=7.0, via=[(4.6, 4.7), (11.6, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "WILL", (9.4, -4.4), delay=0.45, speed=4.8)
    if keys_guard:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 1.9), speed=0.8, delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (10.0, 0.4), speed=5.0, delay=0.1)
    else:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 2.6), speed=3.2, delay=0.2)
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.9, 0.6), speed=4.0, delay=0.3)
    p.pass_to("Y", t=2.0)
    return p


P_PA_BACK, P_PA_GUARD = pa_play(False), pa_play(True)


def pa_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    if t < 0.05:
        key = "RG" if play is P_PA_GUARD else "RB"
        eyes(fld, play, play.position("MIKE", t), play.position(key, t))
    if play is P_PA_GUARD:                    # the key: the right guard, ringed; he never gets past the line
        d, w = play.position("RG", t)
        x, y = _P(fld, play, d, w)
        fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.95, fc="none", ec=GREEN, lw=1.6, zorder=7.5))
        if t > 0.5:
            point_to(fld, play, (2.9, w + 0.6), (d + 0.6, w), "no climb", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.4, shrink=2)
    if t >= 2.0:                              # the throw
        q, y_ = play.position("QB", 2.0), play.position("Y", t + 0.3)
        dashed(fld, play, [tuple(q), tuple(y_)], color=style.BALL, lw=1.2)


animation_or_strip(
    [(P_PA_BACK, 0.0, "keys the back"), (P_PA_BACK, 0.9, ""), (P_PA_BACK, 2.3, ""),
     (P_PA_GUARD, 0.0, "keys the guard"), (P_PA_GUARD, 0.9, ""), (P_PA_GUARD, 2.3, "")],
    notes=["eyes on the back", "the back fakes zone:\nthe Mike steps up", "five yards deep: Y is\nbehind him",
           "eyes on the right guard", "guard fires out, but no\nclimb: not a run", "ten yards deep, in the\ncrosser's path"],
    rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-9.0, 7.6), window=(-7.9, 15.4), after=pa_marks,
    ncols=3, width_in=6.2)
```

Two things in @fig-pa-keys are worth remembering. First, the linebacker who keys the back is not a bad
linebacker; he is doing exactly what he is trained to do against the run, and on most snaps it is the right
call. That is why, as [04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) showed, play-action
works about as well for teams that run the ball badly as for teams that run it well: the linebacker is reacting
to *action*, not to statistics. Second, the cure is in the keys, and it costs something. A linebacker who waits
for the guard to climb is a fraction of a second slower on every real run. Defenses decide, sometimes play by
play, which mistake they would rather make: in obvious running situations the linebackers trigger fast, and in
play-action situations (first down and second-and-short, the shot zones near midfield, against a team that
loves the fake) they read a beat longer.

The Will in @fig-pa-keys is drawn the same way in both rows, for a reason: the fake goes away from him, and a
backside linebacker's run job is to shuffle over the top and wait for the cutback, so a fake to the other side
moves him less. The test, and the cost, fall on the Mike.

## Linebackers as pressure players

The last job is going forward on a pass play. Linebackers have traditionally been the most common extra
rushers, the [blitzers](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-blitz), because they start close to the line and in
the middle, where a rusher reaches the quarterback fastest (modern defenses send their nickel backs and
safeties too). Their pressure roles, all built in Part 7, come in a few recognizable shapes:

- **The A-gap blitz.** Both inside linebackers walk up into the gaps on either side of the center before the
  snap, the [double A-gap mug](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-a-gap-mug), threatening the quickest path
  to the quarterback. The offense has to account for both; the defense may send both, one, or neither and drop
  them into coverage at the snap ([Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)).
- **The green dog (or hug, or add-on).** A linebacker assigned to cover the running back who, when the back
  stays in to block, rushes instead: there is nobody left for him to cover.
- **The simulated pressure.** A linebacker rushes while a defensive lineman drops into coverage, so the offense
  sees five threats but gets four rushers from unexpected places:
  [simulated pressure](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-simulated-pressure), in
  [Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd).
- **The spy.** Against a quarterback who runs, a linebacker is assigned to mirror him, staying at linebacker
  depth and following him wherever he goes: a [spy](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy), covered in
  [Third Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd). Against the fastest quarterbacks, teams
  often spy with a safety or the nickel back instead, for the same speed reason the Sam lost his job.

Every one of these trades coverage for pressure, or pressure for coverage, and the linebacker is the piece the
defense moves to make the trade.

## The part-time Sam and the safety-sized linebacker

Put the jobs together, the run fits, the zone drops, the man coverage on backs and tight ends, the blitzes, and
you can see the problem the modern NFL created for linebackers. Offenses spread out. The more snaps an offense
plays with three wide receivers, the more snaps one of those receivers is in the slot, and the more often the
defense has to choose between a linebacker who walks out over him (@fig-apex-2x2) and a defensive back who
replaces that linebacker.

For most of the last two decades, defenses chose the defensive back. By Pro Football Focus's count, base
defense (four defensive backs, three linebackers) was on the field for 54% of plays in 2008 and 45% in 2011,
and by 2014 defenses had five or more defensive backs out for more than 60% of plays.[^basehist] The
linebacker they removed was usually the Sam, the strong-side linebacker built to take on tight ends and
fullbacks, because the 11-personnel offenses that spread the field had one tight end and no fullback for him
to take on. The nickel package, five defensive backs and two linebackers, became the real base defense of the
NFL, as [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) showed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sam-size
#| fig-cap: "Two trends. Left: how many defensive backs NFL defenses had on the field, as a share of regular-season snaps (nflverse participation data; 2016-2022 from NFL Next Gen Stats personnel labels, 2023-2025 counted from FTN's position lists, so the dashed line marks a change of source). Base defense, four defensive backs and so three linebackers, fell to about a fifth of snaps by 2023 and came back to about 30% in 2025, as offenses returned to two-tight-end sets. Right: the average NFL Combine weight of off-ball linebackers by draft class (2000-2018: players listed as inside linebackers; 2019 on: players listed as linebackers, with edge rushers listed separately; the 2020 and 2021 classes are left out because their data lumps edge rushers in with linebackers). The labels changed in 2019 too, so read the trend, not the step."
style.apply()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
for k, lab, c in (("nickel", "5 DBs (nickel)", style.SERIES[0]), ("base", "4 or fewer (base)", style.SERIES[1]),
                  ("dime", "6 or more (dime)", style.SERIES[2])):
    ax.plot(PKG.index, PKG[k], marker="o", ms=3, lw=2.2 if k == "base" else 1.6, color=c)
    ax.text(2025.3, PKG[k].iloc[-1], lab, fontsize=7.0, va="center", color=style.INK_2)
ax.axvline(2022.5, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.set_xlim(2015.6, 2029.6); ax.set_ylim(0, 85)
ax.set_xticks([2016, 2019, 2022, 2025])
ax.text(2016.0, 83, "for scale: base was on 54% of\nplays in 2008, 45% in 2011 (PFF)", fontsize=6.6,
        color=style.INK_2, va="top")
ax.set_ylabel("Share of defensive snaps (%)")
ax.set_title("Defensive backs on the field, 2016-2025", fontsize=9)
ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(CMB.loc[:2018].index, CMB.loc[:2018, "wt"], marker="o", ms=3, lw=1.8, color=style.SERIES[1])
ax.plot(CMB.loc[2019:2019].index, CMB.loc[2019:2019, "wt"], marker="o", ms=3, lw=0, color=style.SERIES[1])
ax.plot(CMB.loc[2022:].index, CMB.loc[2022:, "wt"], marker="o", ms=3, lw=1.8, color=style.SERIES[1])
ax.axvline(2018.5, color=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.set_ylim(225, 250)
ax.text(2001, 247.6, "listed ILB", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(2019.4, 242.4, "listed LB", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_xticks([2000, 2008, 2016, 2024])
ax.set_ylabel("Pounds")
ax.set_title("Off-ball linebackers at the Combine", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

The left half of @fig-sam-size picks the story up in 2016, after that big drop, and its most recent chapter
is a partial rebound. In 2016 base defense was on the field for `{python} f"{PKG.loc[2016, 'base']:.0f}"`% of
snaps; by 2023 it was down to `{python} f"{PKG.loc[2023, 'base']:.0f}"`%. Then it came back:
`{python} f"{PKG.loc[2025, 'base']:.0f}"`% in 2025, close to the 29.7% Next Gen Stats measured, because offenses
returned to two-tight-end and fullback sets and defenses answered with bigger personnel.[^ngsbase] The Sam
didn't disappear; he became a part-time player.

The other half of the story is the linebackers who stayed. If two linebackers are going to be on the field for
most snaps, and those two have to cover running backs and tight ends in space as well as fill gaps, teams want
them faster, and faster usually means lighter. The right half of @fig-sam-size shows the trend at the NFL
Combine. Off-ball linebackers in the 2000–2009 draft classes averaged `{python} f"{EARLY['wt'].mean():.0f}"`
pounds and ran the 40-yard dash in `{python} f"{EARLY['forty'].mean():.2f}"` seconds; the classes since 2019
have averaged `{python} f"{LATE['wt'].mean():.0f}"` pounds and `{python} f"{LATE['forty'].mean():.2f}"`
seconds.[^combine] Nine or ten pounds and a tenth and a half of a second doesn't sound like much. At the second level it
is the difference between running with a running back and watching him.

The clearest sign of the shift is where some linebackers come from. In 2015 the Arizona Cardinals moved Deone
Bucannon, a safety they had drafted in the first round a year earlier, to inside linebacker, at about 211
pounds. Their depth chart listed him as "$ILB," and the coaches called him the *moneybacker*: a safety's speed
and coverage in a linebacker's spot, playing the run by beating blockers to the hole rather than taking them
on.[^bucannon] Other teams followed with safety-sized linebackers and linebacker-sized safeties, until in some
defenses the line between the two positions is mostly a matter of which word is on the depth chart. The big
nickel of [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), with a
third safety in the box, is the same idea from the other direction.

What the safety-sized linebacker gives up is the thing the Sam was built for: taking on a fullback or a pulling
guard in the hole and holding his ground. A 215-pound linebacker who has to stand still and absorb a 315-pound
guard loses. So the modern linebacker is coached to *not* stand still: to beat the blocker to the spot, or run
through the gap before he arrives, the fits from earlier in this chapter. The best of today's linebackers
combine both. San Francisco's Fred Warner, a third-round pick in 2018 and first-team All-Pro in 2020, 2022, 2023
and 2024, is about 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds: the coverage linebacker teams hoped the safety-sized linebacker would
be, in a full-sized body. Watch him carry a tight end up the seam in his zone drops, the hook/curl seam carry of
@fig-hook-curl, and then fill against the run.[^warner] And when offenses go heavy,
with two tight ends and a fullback, as many did again in 2025, defenses bring back a third linebacker, or a
bigger one. The Sam isn't extinct. He is a specialist who comes in when the offense does.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Linebackers are the defense's run-stoppers; the defensive backs cover." In the modern NFL the two off-ball
linebackers are on the field for most passing snaps and are in coverage on most of them, against running backs,
tight ends and slot receivers. A linebacker who cannot cover cannot stay on the field, however well he tackles.
That, more than anything, is what has changed about the position.
:::

## The green dot: the defense's quarterback

One linebacker usually has one more job, and it starts before anyone moves. Since 2008 NFL rules have allowed
one defensive player on the field to have a radio speaker in his helmet, the way quarterbacks have since 1994;
the owners approved it by a single vote over the required majority.[^radio] That player wears the
[green dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) sticker you met in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), and the radio cuts off with 15
seconds on the play clock. On most teams, he is the Mike.

```{python}
#| label: fig-green-dot
#| fig-cap: "What the green-dot linebacker does before a snap (an illustrative sequence; the words differ from team to team). Against a trips formation with the tight end attached on the right, the Mike (green ring) hears the call in his helmet and relays it, then sets the defense to the formation he sees: the strength, the front, the coverage, then any adjustment to a motion or shift, and the alerts from the week's film study."
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
axf = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.56, 1.0])
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), te(+1),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, 10.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 1.4), will=(4.7, -1.8)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 4.8, 7.8, "$"), D("SS", "S", 8.0, 5.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 13.0, -2.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("MIKE", color=GREEN)
f = draw(p, ax=axf, width_in=3.7, lateral=(-17.6, 17.6), window=(-7.4, 16.4), title=False)
point_to(f, p, (9.6, -6.0), (5.0, 1.0), "green dot:\n\"Strength right! Under!\"", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.0, shrink=8)
say(f, p, -3.6, 9.6, "TE and trips: strong side", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
axt = fig.add_axes([0.58, 0.04, 0.41, 0.92]); axt.axis("off")
steps = [("The call", "Hears it from the coordinator,\nrelays it in the huddle or by signal."),
         ("Strength", "\"Strength right!\" Where is the\nTE? The trips? Sets every rule."),
         ("Front", "\"Under!\" The line sets off the\nstrength: the 3-technique goes away."),
         ("Coverage", "Who has whom: the trips, the\nback, the tight end."),
         ("Adjust and alert", "Motion or shift: re-set it.\n\"Watch the screen!\" \"Boot!\"")]
for i, (h, b) in enumerate(steps):
    y = 0.95 - i * 0.195
    axt.text(0.0, y, str(i + 1), fontsize=8, color="white", fontweight="bold", va="top",
             bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.25", fc=GREEN, ec="none"))
    axt.text(0.11, y + 0.005, h, fontsize=8.4, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="top")
    axt.text(0.11, y - 0.055, b, fontsize=7.3, color=style.INK_2, va="top", linespacing=1.25)
plt.show()
```

What does he actually do with it?

1. **He relays the call.** The defensive coordinator calls the front, the coverage and any pressure into one
   helmet. The green dot passes it to the other ten, in a huddle or with hand signals, before the radio goes
   dead.
2. **He sets the strength.** Every rule in the call depends on which side is "strong," and the strength
   depends on what the offense shows: the tight end, the trips side, the running back, or the wide side of
   the field. The green dot decides and shouts it, and the front sets off his word, the way
   [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd) showed. The hard part is that many defenses set the *front* to the
   tight end (or the back) and the *coverage* to the receivers. In @fig-green-dot they agree; against trips
   with the tight end on the other side they don't, and he has to call both: "Front left, coverage right."
3. **He adjusts to what the offense does.** When the offense shifts or sends a man in motion, the strength may
   change, and with it the front and the coverage rules. With the radio already off, the green dot is the one
   who re-sets everyone, in a second or two, with a word. (If the offense substitutes after the radio has
   cut out, a new call comes from the sideline by hand signal, and he passes it on.)
4. **He makes the alerts.** Linebackers study opponents' tendencies all week. The green dot is the one who
   sees a formation and yells "Watch the screen!" or "Boot! Boot!" before the snap, from a list built in film
   study.
5. **He plays a game with the protection.** The offense's center identifies a defender as the "Mike" for its
   blocking count, the [Mike identification](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-identification) of
   [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd). The defense knows it. Linebackers walk
   up, back out and swap spots before the snap to make that identification wrong.

It is a lot to ask of one player, and it is why teams prize linebackers who are, in the clichéd but accurate
phrase, coaches on the field. It is also why the green dot has started to move. A linebacker who comes off the
field in some packages takes the radio with him, and the backup green dot has to take over. More and more teams
have given the radio to a safety or another defensive back who never leaves the field: six teams did in 2021,
according to one count.[^greendotdb] The Mike's job doesn't vanish when he loses the dot; he still sets the
front and the run fits in the box, while the safety with the radio runs the coverage.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2000"}
**The season:** Ray Lewis's Ravens allowed `{python} f"{int(BAL00.pa.sum())}"` points in 16 games, the fewest
in a 16-game season, and `{python} f"{int(RUSH00['BAL'])}"` rushing yards, also a 16-game record, then beat
the Giants 34–7 in Super Bowl XXXV; Lewis was the game's MVP and the league's Defensive Player of the
Year.[^ravens2000]

**Where to look:** Super Bowl XXXV, against the Giants. **What to notice:** the two big defensive tackles in
front of him, Tony Siragusa and Sam Adams. Their job was to occupy both guards so that nobody could climb to
Lewis: watch the guards at the snap, then watch how often Lewis gets to the ball without anyone touching him.
This is the *protected* linebacker at his best (the opposite of the open linebacker over a free guard): two
big tackles who keep the guards off him, and a linebacker fast enough to his keys to make that pay.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Carolina Panthers 2015"}
**The season:** the Panthers went 15–1 and reached Super Bowl 50 with Luke Kuechly at middle linebacker, three
seasons after he was the Defensive Rookie of the Year and two after he became the youngest Defensive Player of
the Year. In the playoffs that January he returned interceptions for touchdowns in both of Carolina's NFC
games, the first in the opening minutes against Seattle and the second in the 49–15 NFC Championship win over
Arizona.[^kuechly]

**Where to look:** the NFC Championship Game against Arizona. **What to notice:** Kuechly's first step. He was
famous for moving before the play had declared itself, and on the replay you can usually see why: his eyes are
on a guard or the back, and he goes where they tell him. On passing downs, watch him in the hole, reading the
quarterback and driving on throws in front of him. He retired in January 2020,
at 28.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2022"}
**The trade:** On October 31, 2022, Chicago traded Roquan Smith, the eighth pick of the 2018 draft, to Baltimore
for a second-round pick, a fifth-round pick and a linebacker; in January 2023 the Ravens signed him to a
five-year, $100 million extension, the first for an off-ball linebacker at $20 million a year.[^roquan] In the
eight games before he arrived, the Ravens allowed `{python} f"{PRE.pa.mean():.1f}"` points a game; in the nine
after, `{python} f"{POST.pa.mean():.1f}"`. (Not all of that was Smith: other starters returned from injuries,
and the schedule changed. But the timing was hard to miss.)[^ravens22]

**Where to look:** his first game for Baltimore, a 27–13 win at New Orleans on Monday night, November 7.
**What to notice:** a modern run-through linebacker. Watch Smith's fills against zone runs: he is through the
gap before the climbing lineman gets there, which is how a 235-pound linebacker beats a guard who outweighs him
by 80 pounds. Then watch him and Patrick Queen, the other inside linebacker that season, talk before the snap,
and how often they swap responsibilities after the offense shifts.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Mirror the Mike.** For ten snaps, watch only the middle linebacker. Ignore the ball.

- **Before the snap:** Where is he standing: stacked behind a lineman, open over a guard, or walked out over a
  receiver? Is he pointing and shouting? (That's the green dot setting the strength.) Does anyone walk up into
  the A gaps?
- **At the snap: first steps forward or back?** His very first step is a short read step; the *second* one
  tells you what he saw. Forward, it's a run, or he thinks it is. Back, it's a pass. Sideways means he has read
  a pull or zone flow; see which way he goes and where the ball goes.
- **On runs:** Did he fill, plug, scrape or run through? Did a guard get to him? Was he inside the ball as
  he pursued, or did the back cut back behind him?
- **On passes:** Did he drop to a spot, run with a back or a tight end, or rush? On play-action, count his
  steps forward before he turned around.
- **On the replay:** Watch the guards and the back, his keys. Did they tell the truth?

For your prediction log ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
write *F* or *B* for the Mike's first real step, then *run* or *pass*. After a half, check how often his first step
was right, and which plays fooled him.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. The back says one thing, the linemen another.** First-and-10, shotgun, the back to the quarterback's
right. In the first quarter-second after the snap the back takes a step to his *right*, while the right guard
and right tackle pull to the *left*. You are the Mike. Which way do you go, and what is the play?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: the first quarter-second. The back steps right (short arrow); the right guard and right tackle step flat to the left behind the line (their pulls); the left side of the line blocks down to the right, and the tight end steps back. The Mike (ringed) is reading the back and the right guard (dotted)."
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.2, "R")]
p = Play(off, nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 0.2), will=(4.7, -2.2)), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Drill 1: the back steps right, two linemen pull left")
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.5, 3.6), "run")
go_to(p, "RG", (-1.5, -0.8), via=[(-1.5, 1.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (-1.9, 1.0), via=[(-1.8, 2.8)])
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
    q = p.players[k]
    go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.4, q.w + 0.9), "block")
go_to(p, "Y", (-1.6, 5.0), "block")              # hinge: step back and wall off the backside end
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.read("RB", key="MIKE"); p.read("RG", key="MIKE")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-9.0, 9.6), window=(-7.6, 7.6))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Go left, with the guard and tackle. It's counter.** The back's step to the right is the counter step, the lie
the play is built on ([Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)); the two pullers are
the truth, because two linemen can't run to the left unless the ball is going there. The guard will kick out the
end man on the left, and the tackle will wrap through the hole looking for the play-side linebacker, the Will.
(On the right, the tight end steps back to wall off the end the pulling tackle left: a *hinge*.)

You are the backside linebacker. Your guard has just pulled, so you follow him: sideways toward the offense's
left (your right), flat and inside-out, while the center or left guard tries to climb to you, and you fill the
hole the tackle leads through. It is the read in @fig-key-pull, from the other side. A Mike who believes the back
takes a false step toward him, and by the time he recovers the hole has opened behind his back. This is the
textbook case for "if your keys disagree, believe the linemen."
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. The walk-out that gives it away.** Third-and-6. The offense is in 11 personnel with the back beside
the quarterback. Before the snap the back motions out of the backfield and lines up wide on the left. The Will
linebacker walks out with him and stands over him. What did the defense just tell you, and what is the offense
likely to do?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the back (R) motions out to the left, between the slot receiver (H) and the split end (X); the Will (ringed) walks out of the box and follows him (dashed). One deep safety; the cornerbacks and the nickel back are tight on their receivers."
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -17.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.6, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 1.0), will=(4.7, -2.0)) + [
    D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "S", 7.6, 6.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 13.5, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 3.0, -17.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 3.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: the back goes out, the Will goes with him")
p.motion("RB", to=(-1.5, -12.8))
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-20.4, 18.4), window=(-7.6, 16.4))
dashed(f, p, [(4.6, -2.9), (4.4, -8.0), (4.0, -12.0)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
ghost(f, p, 4.0, -12.8, "W")
say(f, p, 9.2, -12.8, "the Will\nends up here", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The defense told you it is in man coverage, and it told you which matchup the offense now has: a running back
against a linebacker, in space, on third down.** A zone defense would have let the back go and simply re-set its
zones; a defense that sends a specific defender with a man who moves is matching him (the motion-as-indicator
idea from [Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)). With one deep safety,
the coverage is probably Cover 1.

The offense will usually go to that matchup: a quick route for the back, a slant, a quick out or an option route,
where his quickness against a linebacker who has never covered him from out there is worth six yards. It is the
case for linebackers who can cover, and for the safety-sized linebackers who replaced the Sam. Two smaller
points: the box has lost a defender, leaving five (four linemen and the Mike) against six blockers, so a quarterback draw is suddenly
attractive; and a well-coached defense may answer the motion by swapping assignments ("banjo," or switching the
nickel back onto the back) so that the linebacker never ends up out there at all. A [banjo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-banjo)
is the general version: two defenders trade who covers whom depending on where the receivers go.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Both linebackers flow.** First-and-10. Outside zone to the right: the line steps right together, and
the back sprints for the tight end's outside leg. The picture is frozen 0.8 seconds after the snap; compare it
with the fast-flow half of @fig-flow. Both
linebackers have flowed hard to the right. Where does the back go, and who made the mistake?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: outside zone right, 0.8 seconds after the snap (simulated; every player is drawn where he is at that moment, and the faint lines are where he has been). The line has stepped right and is cutting off the backside linemen; the back is pressing the edge; the Mike and the Will (ringed) have both run hard to the right, the Will level with the Mike. The shaded area behind the backside of the line is empty."
off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
p = Play(off, over_front(+1), los=40, to_go=10)
T_FREEZE = 0.8


def by(key, end, via=(), kind="path"):
    """Move `key` so that he arrives at `end` exactly at T_FREEZE."""
    pts = [tuple(p._cur(key)), *via, end]
    go_to(p, key, end, kind, speed=max(path_len(pts) / T_FREEZE, 0.1), via=via)


for k in OL_KEYS + ("Y",):
    q = p.players[k]
    by(k, (q.d + 0.3, q.w + 1.2), kind="block")
by("QB", (-2.6, 1.6))
by("RB", (-3.6, 4.6), via=[(-5.9, 2.6)], kind="run")
p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
by("MIKE", (3.6, 5.3), via=[(4.2, 2.8)])
by("WILL", (3.6, 3.3), via=[(4.3, 0.2)])
by("SAM", (2.0, 7.8))
by("NT", (1.2, 0.3)); by("WE", (1.0, -3.4)); by("DT", (1.2, 2.9)); by("SE", (1.2, 4.6))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
LAT3, WIN3 = (-8.6, 10.6), (-8.8, 8.2)
fld = panel(ax, p, tracking(p), T_FREEZE, LAT3, WIN3, rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)))
lane(fld, p, -3.6, 0.4, 1.9, 6.4, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10)
say(fld, p, 5.0, -1.6, "backside:\nnobody home", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
ax.set_title(f"Drill 3: outside zone, {T_FREEZE:.1f} s after the snap", fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK,
             fontweight="bold")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The back cuts back, behind the Will, into the backside A or B gap, and the Will made the mistake.** Outside
zone is built to make the defense run sideways and then to cut against the flow
([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)). The play-side linebacker, the Mike, is right to run
with it, inside-out. But the Will is the backside linebacker, and his job against fast flow is to follow a step
behind the Mike and a little deeper, *over the top*, as the cutback player (@fig-flow). Here he is level with the
Mike and nearly as far over as the ball, so the shaded area behind the line's flow is empty except for linemen
who are being cut off. The back plants his foot and goes there, and the next defender is a safety.

A good Will gives up a yard or two to the outside to keep the cutback: if the back keeps going, the Mike and the
Sam are there, and the Will arrives late but in the right place. He doesn't hold the cutback alone; the backside
end has to squeeze or chase so the back can't bend it all the way back. The cutback runs you see go for 20 yards
are usually a backside player out of place: a linebacker who ran too fast, an end who got reached or cut, or a
safety who flowed too early.
:::
:::

## Back to the huddle

The chapter opened with a middle linebacker who went the "wrong" way, away from the back's jab step, and
stopped the run for no gain, while the analyst circled the left guard. Now you can see what he saw. The guard
nearest him fired out (a run), and the left guard opened his hips and ran flat behind the line (a pull, so a
gap-scheme run going where he went). The back's jab step was window dressing. The Mike went with the puller, had
the shorter trip, and met him at the line, where the hole was supposed to be. The back never had a chance to
choose.

## Takeaways

- **Where a linebacker stands is a trade.** Stacked behind a lineman, he is shielded and hard to read but a step
  slower to the gaps; open over an uncovered guard, he sees everything and is easy to block; walked out to an apex over a slot receiver, he can
  cover but he has left the box light and become the offense's conflict defender.
- **Linebackers read keys, not the ball.** The guards' first steps (fire out, down block, pull, zone step, pass
  set) and the near back's direction tell him run or pass and where, early enough to get there. The offense knows it, which is
  why counters, traps and play-action are built to make his keys lie.
- **Flow tells him how to move; the fit tells him where.** Fast flow: run with it, inside-out, with the backside
  linebacker a step behind for the cutback. Slow flow: press the gap and stay square. The fit is a fill, a plug, a
  scrape or a run-through, and the scrape is also the defense's answer to the zone read.
- **The second level is where runs are decided.** Pursuit angles aim where the runner will be, a step inside him,
  with a leverage player outside; leverage tackling takes away one direction and wraps the legs. Inside linebackers
  make a fifth to a quarter of the tackles on runs up to 9 yards; misses rise with the space around the tackle,
  and a run that beats the linebackers is a defensive back's tackle.
- **On passes, linebackers are hook/curl defenders, man defenders on backs and tight ends, robbers in the hole and
  blitzers.** Play-action targets their keys; the uncovered guard who doesn't climb is the tell.
- **The position has shrunk.** Spread offenses made the Sam a part-time player, replaced by a nickel back, and made
  the remaining linebackers lighter and faster, down to safety-sized "moneybackers." The green-dot linebacker, who sets the
  strength and adjusts the defense before every snap, is the job that hasn't changed.

    (`nflreadpy.load_pfr_advstats(stat_type="def")`), seasons 2021–2025: missed tackles divided by combined tackles
    plus missed tackles, summed over each group, with the group taken from the nflverse roster's
    `depth_chart_position` that season (`{python} f"{MISS_MATCH:.0f}"`% of player-seasons match a roster entry;
    "DB" is counted with the cornerbacks). The code is in this chapter's source.

[^ngsbase]: James Reber (Next Gen Stats), "NFL trend watch: heavy personnel could shape Super Bowl LX showdown
    between Patriots and Seahawks," NFL.com (base defense on 29.7% of snaps in 2025, up from 20.5% in 2023):
    <https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-trend-watch-heavy-personnel-could-shape-super-bowl-lx-showdown-between-patriots-and-seahawks>.
    The chart is a course calculation from nflverse participation data (`defense_personnel`), regular-season runs
    and passes, which differs slightly from NGS's own figures.

[^basehist]: Mike Clay, Pro Football Focus, "Defensive personnel packages, part 1" (April 11, 2012): "A base
    defense was in place on 54% of all plays back in 2008, but that figure fell to 52% in 2009, 48% in 2010, and 45% in
    2011": <https://www.pff.com/fantasy-defensive-personnel-packages-%25e2%2580%2593-part-1/>. The 2014 figure (five or
    more defensive backs on 60.3% of plays) is PFF data reported by Peter King (*The MMQB*), as quoted in CBS Sports,
    "Here's why the nickel defense is the new base defense in the NFL" (April 4, 2016):
    <https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/heres-why-the-nickel-defense-is-the-new-base-defense-in-the-nfl>.

[^combine]: Course calculation from nflverse NFL Combine data (`load_combine`): players listed "ILB" for the 2000–2018
    draft classes and "LB" from 2019, when the data lists most edge rushers separately as "EDGE." The 2020 and 2021
    files have no "EDGE" label (their "LB" rows include edge rushers such as Darrell Taylor, 267 pounds), so those
    two classes are left out. Forty-yard times are averaged over the players who ran. Because the labels changed in 2019, part of the drop between the two
    periods may be a change in who is counted.

[^bucannon]: NFL.com, "'Moneybacker' Deone Bucannon key to Cardinals' D" (2015), with Bucannon at 6-foot-1 and 211

    he plays": <https://www.nfl.com/news/moneybacker-deone-bucannon-key-to-cardinals-d-0ap3000000597969>. The
    move came in 2015 training camp, after inside linebacker Sean Weatherspoon was hurt; Bucannon had started at
    strong safety as a 2014 rookie (27th pick): "Deone Bucannon," Wikipedia,

[^radio]: Patriots.com, "Adoption of defensive communication passes by one vote" (2008), and NFL.com, "Niners give

    <https://www.nfl.com/news/niners-give-good-reviews-to-headsets-for-defenders-09000d5d80822daa>.

[^greendotdb]: Kaelen Jones, "The Future of NFL Defenses Lies in a Lime-Green Dot," *The Ringer* (March 7, 2022):
